title: A coanalytic upper bound for fair almost-sure termination
formal: Does fair almost-sure termination for finitely branching probabilistic nondeterministic Turing machines admit a computable many-one reduction to well-foundedness of primitive-recursive trees on \(\mathbb N\)? That is, is there one total computable map sending each machine/input pair \((M,w)\) to such a tree \(T_{M,w}\) with \(M\) terminating with probability one under every fair scheduler exactly when \(T_{M,w}\) has no infinite branch?
why: The target locates how much logical complexity fairness adds to probabilistic termination. A reduction to well-founded trees would connect general FAST reasoning to the established coanalytic framework; a negative answer would show that those certificates cannot cover this model through any computable translation.
status_note: The July 2025 source leaves the complexity of its strong-fairness FAST model unspecified. The card explicitly selects the coanalytic upper-bound variant, rather than attributing it verbatim to the source author. The checked PAST classification and 2026 weak-fairness rules do not establish it; no matching general reduction or impossibility theorem was located in the bounded September 2026 check.

sentences: The machine combines finite nondeterministic choices with rational probabilistic choices and unbounded tape memory.
Schedulers may use arbitrary histories, but must satisfy strong fairness on every supported infinite execution.
FAST requires probability-one termination under each such fair scheduler, without an expected-runtime bound.
This card selects the precise question of a computable reduction to well-foundedness of primitive-recursive trees.
Known results for positive almost-sure termination and weakly fair distributed protocols have different hypotheses.

definitions: A machine has a finite control, a finite tape alphabet with a blank symbol, one unbounded tape initially containing the finite input \(w\), and a head position. Nonhalting control states are probabilistic or nondeterministic. Each has a fixed finite nonempty set of actions. An action is a total finite table indexed by the currently scanned symbol, prescribing a symbol to write, a head move by at most one cell and the next control state. Thus an available action is enabled whenever its origin control state is visited. A probabilistic state also has a fixed rational distribution of strictly positive probabilities over its actions; these choices are sampled independently conditional on the execution history. Deterministic behavior is represented by a single action of probability one. Halting states have no actions. A scheduler is any function from finite execution histories ending at a nondeterministic state to an available action. Histories include the configurations and actions taken. Schedulers are deterministic but need not be computable and may use the entire history. A scheduler is fair from the given initial configuration if, on every infinite execution consistent with it and the probabilistic action supports, every nondeterministic action whose origin state occurs infinitely often is itself taken infinitely often. This is pathwise strong fairness, including individual infinite paths of probability zero. The scheduler induces the usual probability measure on executions, with finite-prefix probabilities given by products of the rational choices. Fair almost-sure termination (FAST) means that every fair scheduler gives probability one to reaching a halting state. It imposes no bound on expected running time. Machine tables, rational probabilities and input words have finite binary encodings. A tree on \(\mathbb N\) is a prefix-closed subset of finite sequences of natural numbers. It is presented by a primitive-recursive membership predicate: a finite expression built from zero, successor and projections using composition and primitive recursion, with a fixed effective encoding of sequences. An infinite branch is a function \(b:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N\) whose every finite prefix belongs to the tree. Well-foundedness means no such branch exists. Branching is not restricted to two children or any fixed finite bound. The reduction must halt on every valid machine/input pair and output a valid predicate for a prefix-closed tree; no resource bound on the reduction is required.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of a total computable reduction satisfying the displayed equivalence for all machine/input pairs, or prove in Lean that no such reduction exists. Requiring computable schedulers, fairness only with probability one, weak fairness, finite expected time, or finitely branching witness trees changes the problem. Sound proof rules for selected program classes alone do not establish this universal reduction.

context_blocks.text: The source asks both for the recursion-theoretic complexity of FAST and for sound complete reasoning techniques. Editorial specialization: this card selects the coanalytic upper-bound question, expressed concretely as a reduction to tree well-foundedness. It does not present a conjectured upper bound as a theorem or claim that this choice already supplies a Hoare-style proof system.

Fairness rules out indefinitely ignoring an action at a control state revisited infinitely often. It still permits arbitrarily long finite postponements. Requiring this property on every supported infinite execution is stronger than requiring that unfair executions merely have probability zero.

The source reports \(\Pi^1_1\)-completeness for the corresponding non-probabilistic fair-termination problem. Well-foundedness of recursive, arbitrarily branching trees is the standard complete problem at that coanalytic level; the reduction target makes the prospective upper-bound question precise.

Probability-one termination permits exceptional nonterminating executions of probability zero. It is therefore weaker than termination on every path, even though the scheduler’s fairness requirement in this card quantifies over every supported infinite path. These two uses of quantification must not be conflated.

The 2023 positive-almost-sure-termination work proves a \(\Pi^1_1\)-complete classification for a different property: finite expected runtime for each scheduler, without the same fair-scheduler restriction. That theorem does not automatically classify FAST.

The 2026 distributed-algorithm verification paper supplies sound rules combining probabilistic reasoning with weak fairness and applies them to consensus protocols. Those applications are important evidence of useful techniques, but its stated soundness and fairness convention do not prove the universal strong-fairness reduction requested here.
